summary: Describes an architecture for admission and termination of flows based on pre-congestion information, to protect the quality of service of established inelastic flows such as voice inside a single Diffserv domain.

plainLanguage.summary: Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) marks packets when traffic approaches configured rates below a link's capacity. Network-edge nodes use those marks to decide whether to admit new flows or end some existing flows.

subtitle: An architecture for managing real-time flows using early signs of congestion.

tldr.problem: A Diffserv network needs to protect established inelastic flows, such as real-time voice, when links approach overload. Tracking every flow throughout the network would add complexity to its core.
tldr.mechanism: Interior nodes measure aggregate PCN traffic and mark packets when configured rates are exceeded. Boundary nodes use those marks to block new flows or terminate selected existing flows.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5559 describes the architecture, assumptions, operational issues, and open challenges. It leaves detailed metering, encoding, and boundary-node behavior to other documents.

sections.title: Early Warning for Network Traffic
sections.content:
Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) aims to protect the quality of service of inelastic flows in a single Differentiated Services (Diffserv) domain. Each link measures the aggregate rate of PCN traffic and marks packets when that rate exceeds configured thresholds below the link rate.

Boundary nodes read the marks and use them for two separate functions. Admission control decides whether to allow a new flow; flow termination can remove some existing flows in abnormal conditions so the remaining flows receive better service. The interior of the domain meters aggregate traffic rather than keeping per-flow state.
sections.plainLanguage: PCN marks packets when traffic reaches warning levels below a link's capacity. Nodes at the network edge use those marks to manage new and existing flows.

sections.title: Interior and Boundary Node Roles
sections.content:
PCN-interior-nodes classify PCN packets, measure the total PCN traffic on a link, and mark packets when a meter indicates pre-congestion. They do not need per-flow state. PCN-boundary-nodes control flow admission and termination using marked data packets observed at the edge.

Two rates guide marking. Threshold metering marks all PCN packets when traffic exceeds the lower PCN-threshold-rate. Excess-traffic metering marks an amount of traffic corresponding to the portion above the higher PCN-excess-rate. The RFC describes both a baseline encoding with two states and possible extended encodings with three states.

Admission control and flow termination can be deployed independently or together. With three marking states, both can use separate marks. With two states, the domain can enable either function or use one mark for both with less accurate admission control.
sections.plainLanguage: Interior nodes measure total traffic and mark packets; boundary nodes interpret those marks and make flow decisions. Separate marking states can distinguish the warning for new flows from the stronger warning for existing flows.

sections.title: Admitting and Terminating Flows
sections.content:
For admission control, an egress node can measure the fraction of threshold-marked packets in traffic from a particular ingress node. Depending on the configured approach, the egress or ingress node then admits or blocks the proposed flow. The ingress node polices packets so only admitted traffic enters the domain and flows stay within their agreed profile.

For flow termination, nodes estimate traffic above the supportable rate and choose which existing flows to terminate. The architecture describes alternatives that compare measured rates, respond to excess-traffic marks, or select among marked flows. The decision is made for a particular ingress-egress pair, not necessarily for the whole domain.

Marks travel in packet headers; signaling between boundary nodes carries feedback needed for decisions. The RFC gives RSVP as one possible signaling context but does not require one specific boundary-node behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: When the warning level is high, the network can refuse a new flow. If an abnormal event overloads a link, it can select existing flows to end and protect the others.

sections.title: Tunnels, Failures, and Applicability
sections.content:
PCN markings must remain meaningful when packets cross tunnels inside a PCN domain. The RFC describes copying markings into an outer header during encapsulation and carrying the more severe marking inward during decapsulation. When only one tunnel endpoint is inside the domain, the marking is cleared at the appropriate endpoint to avoid confusing nodes outside the domain.

If an interior node or link fails, routing can move traffic onto a new path. If that path is pre-congested, admission control can stop new flows and flow termination can remove traffic. The RFC assumes a controlled domain of trusted PCN-enabled nodes, inelastic flows with known peak rates, and enough flows on bottleneck links for statistical measurement to work. Emergency use is outside scope.

Open challenges include equal-cost multipath routing, tunnels, coordinating both directions of a session, global coordination among ingress-egress pairs, and sudden surges of admission requests.
sections.plainLanguage: PCN is intended for a controlled domain with trusted nodes and many steady-rate flows. Tunnels and rapid traffic changes can make its measurements and decisions less reliable.

sections.title: Trust and Security
sections.content:
The architecture assumes PCN nodes measure traffic and mark packets truthfully. Ingress nodes must police traffic, and boundary nodes must surround the PCN domain so traffic cannot enter without admission control.

A rogue interior node could mark every packet and prevent admissions, or fail to mark traffic during pre-congestion. Boundary nodes should handle denial-of-service and state-exhaustion attacks, and signaling between them must be protected against spoofing, replay, and man-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: PCN depends on every node in its domain reporting congestion honestly. The boundary nodes must authenticate their signaling and prevent unapproved traffic from entering.
